entry.title: Fair Work Ombudsman v Sadamatsu [2026] FCA 1568
entry.content:
The Fair Work Ombudsman brought proceedings against the sole director of a restaurant company for underpayment of penalty rates, overtime, split shift allowances, annual leave and leave loading, and record-keeping failures. The director failed to file a defence, comply with Court orders or attend hearings, so the Court granted default judgment under r 5.23, treating the pleaded facts as admitted. The Court declared contraventions, ordered compensation and interest, and listed the matter for a penalty hearing.

entry.title: Darlington-Thomas v Elgas Limited [2026] FCA 1566
entry.content:
The Federal Court granted Ms Darlington-Thomas leave under s 46PO(3A)(a) of the Australian Human Rights Commission Act 1986 (Cth) to proceed against her labour hire employer, Zoom, for alleged disability discrimination. The AHRC had terminated her complaint against Zoom, but the Court held the claim was reasonably arguable and should be resolved with the overlapping claim against Elgas.

Key holding: On an application for leave under s 46PO(3A)(a) of the AHRC Act, the Court asks only whether the proposed discrimination claim is reasonably arguable and not fanciful, rather than determining the merits.

I am satisfied that the text, context and purpose of the leave requirement in s 46PO(3A) suggests that it is appropriate for the Court to consider in determining whether to grant leave whether the claims made by an applicant are reasonably arguable, and are - at the least - not fanciful. This is consistent with the language used in s 46P(1A).

entry.title: Shah v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FCA 1560
entry.content:
This was an appeal to the Federal Court from the dismissal of judicial review of a Tribunal decision affirming refusal of a Student (Temporary) (Class TU) visa. The Tribunal found Mr Shah was not a genuine applicant for temporary entry and stay as a student under cl 500.212. The Federal Court dismissed the appeal and ordered costs.

Key holding: Refusing to accept an applicant’s bare assertion that a subjective mandatory criterion is satisfied does not, of itself, establish jurisdictional error.

A decision not to accept a bare assertion by an applicant that a mandatory subjective criterion has been satisfied, does not establish jurisdictional error.

entry.title: Robert Palmer v Keramos Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 3945
entry.content:
In [2026] FWC 3945, Robert Palmer lodged an unfair dismissal application under s 394 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) (FW Act) out of time, and Keramos Pty Ltd objected on jurisdiction. The Fair Work Commission dismissed the application under s 399A after Mr Palmer repeatedly failed to comply with directions and to respond to the employer’s dismissal application. The merits and extension-of-time question were not determined.

Key holding: Under s 399A of the FW Act, the FWC may dismiss an application where an applicant unreasonably fails to comply with FWC directions, on the employer’s application and in the exercise of the FWC’s discretion.

I am satisfied that Mr Palmer has unreasonably failed to comply with directions of the FWC relating to this Application. On the application of Keramos and in the exercise of my discretion under section 399A of the FW Act, I have decided to dismiss the Application.

entry.title: Watson v Director of Public Prosecutions (NSW) [2026] NSWCA 222
entry.content:
Mr Watson sought judicial review in the NSW Court of Appeal of Beckett DCJ’s refusal under s 5B of the Criminal Appeal Act 1912 (NSW) to submit questions of law to the Court of Criminal Appeal after his conviction appeal was dismissed. The Court of Appeal dismissed the amended summons, holding that no jurisdictional error was shown in her Honour’s treatment of the proposed questions. Costs were awarded to the DPP.

Key holding: On judicial review of a s 5B decision, an error by the District Court in characterising a proposed question as law, fact or mixed fact and law is ordinarily an error of law within jurisdiction and therefore not a jurisdictional error.

As a consequence, an error by a judge, when determining an application under s 5B, in characterising a proposed question as a question of law, a question of fact, or a question of mixed law and fact, is ordinarily apt to be characterised as an error of law within jurisdiction.

entry.title: DBHP and CEO, National Disability Insurance Agency (NDIS) [2026] ARTA 2419
entry.content:
DBHP sought review of an NDIS statement of participant supports, challenging the refusal of various supports including support worker hours, respite, meal replacement, nutritional supplements, therapies, dietetics, occupational therapy and speech therapy. The Administrative Review Tribunal, applying s 34 of the National Disability Insurance Scheme Act 2013 (Cth), affirmed the decision under review. The case is DBHP and CEO, National Disability Insurance Agency (NDIS) [2026] ARTA 2419 (20 October 2026).

Key holding: Under s 34(1) of the National Disability Insurance Scheme Act 2013 (Cth), all criteria are cumulative, so if any criterion is not met the support is not reasonable and necessary and cannot be funded in a statement of participant supports.

Subsection 34(1) of the NDIS Act is cumulative, meaning that all the criteria must be met. If any criteria are not met, then the requested support is not reasonable and necessary and cannot be funded under a SOPS.

entry.title: Baraboutis and CEO, National Disability Insurance Agency (NDIS) [2026] ARTA 2417
entry.content:
Ms Baraboutis sought review of a decision refusing her access to the NDIS. The Tribunal accepted she had physical and neurological impairments and that some were permanent, but was not satisfied they caused substantially reduced functional capacity under s 24(1)(c) of the NDIS Act. It affirmed the refusal.

Key holding: In assessing whether impairments result in substantially reduced functional capacity under s 24(1)(c), the Tribunal must consider each specified activity as a whole rather than by reference to isolated tasks.

Further, the requirement to consider an activity as a whole, rather than by reference to tasks considered in isolation (as made plain in the amendment to s 24(1)(c)) reflects the reasoning of the Full Court of the Federal Court in National Disability Insurance Agency v Foster (2023) 295 FCR 521; [2023] FCAFC 11 ('Foster').

entry.title: Lippl and CEO, National Disability Insurance Agency (NDIS) [2026] ARTA 2416
entry.content:
This NDIS review concerned whether Ms Lippl should receive additional 1:1 support worker hours beyond those in her statement of participant supports. The Tribunal was not satisfied the requested additional hours represented value for money, finding her current flexible supports sufficient and an increase risked dependency. It nonetheless set aside and remitted the matter to fix the SoPS wording and specify support-worker assistance in accordance with the orders.

Key holding: Additional requested NDIS support worker hours are not reasonable and necessary where the evidence shows the participant can use current flexible funding to meet needs and increased hours risk dependency, so the value-for-money criterion is not met.

The Tribunal has determined the requested additional support worker hours do not satisfy the statutory requirement of representing value for money and cannot be approved by the Tribunal. The evidence is that Ms Lippl can use her support worker hours flexibly, that the current provision is sufficient to meet her needs and that increasing her hours risks creating dependency on support workers over time.

entry.title: BNE24 v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FCA 1561
entry.content:
This was an appeal from the Federal Circuit and Family Court (Division 2) dismissing review of a Tribunal decision refusing a protection visa. The unrepresented appellant argued the Tribunal’s adverse credibility findings were illogical or unreasonable. The Federal Court dismissed the appeal, holding the primary judge correctly found no jurisdictional error.

Key holding: A Tribunal’s adverse credibility finding does not involve jurisdictional error merely because a reviewing court would have reached a different factual finding; the reasoning must be legally unreasonable.

Therefore, jurisdictional error in the reasoning by the Tribunal as to the credibility of the account given by an applicant is not established by seeking to persuade a court on review that the Tribunal's reasoning includes an error in the sense that the Court would not make the same finding.

entry.title: Australian Securities and Investments Commission v Dawson [2026] FCA 1548
entry.content:
SXHR, a Sri Lankan unauthorised maritime arrival in immigration detention, sought judicial review of a Tribunal decision affirming refusal of a Bridging E visa under s 501(1) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth). The Tribunal had applied Direction No 110 and refused the visa notwithstanding the applicant’s outstanding Ministerial intervention request. The Federal Court dismissed the review.

Key holding: Direction 110 requires comparison of the risk attached to refusal and grant of the visa, but not separate assessment of every possible outcome after grant where only the grant creates a risk of the applicant remaining in the community.

There is no error in that approach; nothing could have been gained by comparing the nature or extent of that risk depending on which of the two identified scenarios following the grant of a visa eventuated. DVRL does not say anything against that.

entry.title: Australian Securities and Investments Commission v Dawson [2026] FCA 1547
entry.content:
This was a judicial review of the Administrative Review Tribunal’s decision affirming non-revocation of Mr Dabea’s visa cancellation under s 501CA(4) after serious child sexual offences. Mr Dabea alleged the Tribunal failed to properly consider impediments if removed to Fiji and denied procedural fairness by sending post-hearing DFAT country information. The Federal Court dismissed the application.

Key holding: On judicial review, a tribunal’s reasons must be read fairly and as a whole, so a failure to evaluate a mandatory consideration is not readily inferred merely because the reasons are brief.

The task on judicial review is to read the reasons fairly and as a whole: see EGH19 v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] HCA 33 at [68] (Gordon, Steward and Gleeson JJ).

entry.title: Paul Campbell v Thiess Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 4087
entry.content:
Mr Campbell was summarily dismissed by Thiess after an incident with a co-worker at the Mount Pleasant mine. He applied for an unfair dismissal remedy under s 394 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth). The decision’s catchwords record a valid reason for dismissal, but that the dismissal was harsh and reinstatement appropriate.

Key holding: A threat of physical violence towards a co-worker, accompanied by offensive language, can give an employer a sound, defensible and well-founded valid reason for dismissal under s 387(a).

Mr Campbell's conduct the subject of allegations 1 to 3, particularly allegations 2 and 3, gave Thiess a sound, defensible and well-founded reason to terminate his employment. It is inappropriate for an employee to threaten another employee at work.

entry.title: Application by Crown Melbourne Limited Trading AS Crown Melbourne [2026] FWC 4086
entry.content:
Crown applied under s 229 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) for bargaining orders restraining the UWU from alleged misrepresentations during its “vote no” campaign and requiring corrective notices. The Commission considered whether the UWU’s communications and bargaining conduct breached s 228(1)(e) and whether bargaining orders were reasonable. The decision records that orders were not made.

Key holding: A union’s different view of the practical consequences of a proposed agreement is not itself a misrepresentation for good faith bargaining purposes.

That the UWU sees the practical consequences of an effective two-tiered wage system differently to Crown, does not in itself make it a misrepresentation.

entry.title: Application by United Workers' Union (108V) [2026] FWC 4066
entry.content:
The UWU applied for bargaining orders to stop a vote on a proposed Coles subsidiary enterprise agreement, alleging CNSCE had breached the good faith bargaining requirements. The Commission found a breach of s 228(1)(b) for failing to provide the draft agreement in time, but refused the orders because it was not reasonable in all the circumstances. Application dismissed.

Key holding: Timely disclosure of an available draft enterprise agreement is relevant information required by s 228(1)(b); however, a breach does not automatically justify a bargaining order because s 230 requires the Commission to be satisfied an order is reasonable in all the circumstances.

The failure to provide it represents a breach of the good faith bargaining obligations. However, for reasons which are explained below, including the UWU's own failure to present bargaining proposals, and failure to identify any issues it had adverted to with the proposed agreement after it received a copy of it ( on 8 October 2026), weigh against it being reasonable in all circumstances to make the orders sought.

entry.title: Application by Mrs Marietna Di Marcantonio [2026] FWC 4081
entry.content:
Mrs Di Marcantonio applied under s 789FC of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) for an order to stop bullying against her former employer and three named individuals. After her employment ended, the Commission considered whether the application should be dismissed because there was no continuing risk of bullying. Deputy President Butler dismissed the application under s 587(1)(c).

Key holding: Where an applicant no longer works with the named persons and there is no foreseeable risk of return, the Commission lacks jurisdiction to make stop-bullying orders and the application has no reasonable prospects of success.

In the absence of any continuing risk and having regard to my consideration above, there is no jurisdiction to make an order to stop bullying. Therefore, the application has no reasonable prospects of success.

entry.title: The Civil Air Operations Officers’ Association Of Australia Trading AS Civil Air v Airservices Australia [2026] FWC 3820
entry.content:
Civil Air applied under s 739 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) for the Fair Work Commission to arbitrate a dispute about redundancy-type benefits under the Airservices Australia (Air Traffic Control and Supporting Air Traffic Services) Enterprise Agreement 2024-2027. The dispute concerned whether air traffic controllers who cannot obtain, or refuse to obtain, a National Security Clearance or Citizenship Eligibility Waiver are entitled to cl 62.13(a)(i)-(ii) benefits on termination.

Key holding: Clause 62.13 termination benefits require the employee to be a “potentially surplus employee” under cl 62.2, and inability or refusal to obtain an NSC or CEW does not make an ATC surplus where the class of ATCs remains required.

For these reasons I do not consider that employees who are unable or refuse to obtain an NSC (or CEW) can qualify for the entitlements in clause 62.13(a)(i) and (ii) because they are in a class of employees formally identified by the Respondent as a class which has a greater number of employees in it that is necessary for its efficient and economical working, within the meaning of clause 62.2(a) of the Agreement.

entry.title: Aurecon Australasia Pty Ltd & Tristan Meo v Jennifer Baker [2026] FWCFB 283
entry.content:
The Full Bench considered an appeal from a decision to issue a certificate under s 368(3) of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) despite Aurecon’s jurisdictional objection that Ms Baker had not been dismissed. The Full Bench held the Commissioner was required to determine that maintained objection before issuing the certificate. Permission to appeal was granted, the appeal allowed, and the certificate quashed.

Key holding: Where a respondent maintains a dispute that an applicant was not dismissed, the Commission must determine that antecedent jurisdictional issue before exercising its powers under s 368 or issuing a s 368(3) certificate.

For those reasons, it was not open to the Commissioner to issue a certificate under s 368(3) without first determining whether Ms Baker had been dismissed.

entry.title: GWN25 by his Litigation Representative the Public Advocate v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FCA 1535
entry.content:
GWN25 sought judicial review of an Administrative Review Tribunal decision affirming refusal to revoke the mandatory cancellation of his visa under s 501CA(4) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth). The Minister conceded jurisdictional error in light of Minister for Immigration and Citizenship v DVRL, and the parties jointly proposed certiorari and mandamus. The Federal Court set aside the Tribunal decision and remitted the matter for redetermination, with costs.

Key holding: When assessing community risk under the relevant ministerial direction, the Tribunal must consider the different levels of risk depending on the visa status the applicant would hold, where that issue is advanced and supported by evidence.

The effect of the full court's ruling in DVRL is that the Tribunal was obliged, when considering "... the risk to the Australian community ..." for the purposes of cl 8.1(2) of the applicable ministerial direction, to consider not merely the risk that the applicant might pose if his permanent visa were restored but also the risk that he might pose as the holder of an ongoing bridging visa.

entry.content:
